items.ex: A sequel is the next part of a story, like Part 2 of a movie or book. People say the sequel to a movie. The opposite is a prequel, which tells what happened before.
exs: Her lash lift was so good, she came back for the sequel: a full set.
The sequel was even funnier than the first movie.

items.ex: I guess means I think, but you're not totally sure. People say I guess so, or I guess you're right. It's casual, and a good way to get a little thinking time.
exs: I guess I'll add a few more lashes on the outer corner.
Are you coming tonight? I guess so, if I finish work early.

items.ex: A hit is something very popular, like a hit song or show. People say it was a big hit, or a hit with someone. The opposite is a flop.
exs: The new lash style was a huge hit with my younger clients.
Your cookies were a hit at the party.

items.ex: Go on a date means to go out with someone you like romantically, for dinner or coffee. People say go on a date with someone, or a first date.
exs: My client is going on a first date tonight, so she wanted her lashes extra pretty.
We went on a date to a small Italian restaurant.

items.zh: 松了一口气的；如释重负的
items.ex: Relieved is the good feeling you get when a worry is over. People say I'm so relieved, or relieved to hear something. The noun is relief: what a relief!
exs: I was so relieved when the client said the lashes didn't irritate her eyes.
She was relieved to hear that her test results were normal.

items.ex: Feel awful about means you feel very sorry or bad about something. People say I feel awful about it, or feel awful about doing something. It sounds sincere.
exs: I feel awful about running late for your appointment.
She felt awful about forgetting her friend's birthday.

items.ex: Make it up to someone means you do something nice after you made a mistake or hurt them. People say let me make it up to you. It's very common and casual.
exs: Sorry I had to reschedule. Let me make it up to you with a free refill.
He forgot our anniversary, so he's making it up to me with dinner.

items.ex: Take someone out means you invite them somewhere, like a restaurant, and often you pay. People say take someone out to dinner. Ask someone out is different: that means ask for a date.
exs: I'm taking my assistant out to lunch to thank her for a busy week.
My dad took us out for ice cream after the game.

items.ex: My treat means I'll pay. People say it's my treat, or dinner's my treat. Another casual way is it's on me. It's friendly and very common with friends.
exs: Coffee's my treat today. You've been such a loyal client.
Put your wallet away. It's my treat.

items.ex: Pick someone up means you go and get them, usually by car. People say pick me up at eight, or pick up the kids. The opposite is drop someone off.
exs: Can you pick me up after my last client at six?
I need to pick up my kids from school.

items.ex: Lovely means very nice or beautiful. People say a lovely evening, or that's lovely. It's warm and a little polite, great for thank-you messages.
exs: Your skin looks lovely today.
Thank you for a lovely evening.

items.ex: I had a great time means I really enjoyed it. People say it after a party, trip, or date. A more excited, casual version is I had a blast.
exs: Thanks for the birthday lunch. I had a great time.
We had a great time at the beach this weekend.

items.ex: I wish means you want something to be different from now. People say I wish I had more time, or I wish I could. Use I hope for things that are really possible.
exs: I wish I could fit you in today, but I'm fully booked.
I wish this weekend would never end.

items.zh: 和平常的任何一天一样
items.ex: Just like any other day means a normal day with nothing special. People often start a story with it, right before something surprising happens.
exs: It started just like any other day, and then a celebrity walked into the salon.
Today felt just like any other Tuesday.

items.ex: Ordinary means normal, nothing special. People say an ordinary day, or ordinary people. Out of the ordinary means unusual. The opposite is extraordinary, which means amazing.
exs: Most of my clients are ordinary working moms who want to save time in the morning.
It was an ordinary Saturday, nothing special.

items.ex: A twist of fate is a surprise event that changes your life. People say by a twist of fate. It sounds a little dramatic, great for telling stories.
exs: By a twist of fate, my first client in the US became my business partner.
In a strange twist of fate, they ended up working at the same company.

items.ex: Crash into means to hit something hard while moving. People say the car crashed into a tree. A crash is also an accident, like a car crash.
exs: A delivery guy almost crashed into my salon door with his bike.
He was looking at his phone and crashed into a tree.

items.zh: 这听起来可能很疯狂，但……
items.ex: This may sound crazy, but is a way to start a surprising idea. It makes your idea feel softer. It's casual and very useful in conversation.
exs: This may sound crazy, but I actually enjoy fixing other artists' lash mistakes.
This may sound crazy, but I'm thinking of moving to Alaska.

items.ex: Fall in love means to start loving someone. People say fall in love with someone, or something, like a city. Be in love is the feeling after that.
exs: I fell in love with lash art the first time I tried it.
They fell in love during college.

items.ex: Layoffs are when a company ends many workers' jobs because of money problems. The verb is lay off: they laid off fifty people. It's different from being fired for poor work.
exs: A lot of my new clients work in tech, and some are worried about layoffs.
After the layoffs, the office felt very quiet.

items.ex: Be supposed to means something is expected or planned. People say I'm supposed to be at work, or he was supposed to call. Often the plan didn't happen.
exs: You're not supposed to get your lashes wet for the first day.
He was supposed to call me last night, but he forgot.

items.ex: Destiny means what will happen in your future, as if it's already decided. People say it was destiny, or we were meant to meet. It sounds romantic and a bit serious.
exs: Some clients joke that finding my studio was destiny.
They believe it was destiny that they met.

items.zh: 说点开心的；换个轻松的话题
items.ex: On a happier note is a way to change from a sad topic to a good one. People also say on a lighter note. It makes conversation sound smooth.
exs: It's been a slow month. On a happier note, I just got two new regular clients.
The weather was terrible. On a happier note, the food was amazing.

items.ex: Guess what is a fun way to start sharing surprising news. The other person usually says, what? It's casual and friendly, best with friends and family, or in a story.
exs: Guess what? I'm fully booked for the next two weeks!
Guess what happened at work today?

items.ex: Generous means happy to give money, time, or help. People say she's very generous, or that's generous of you. The opposite is stingy, or cheap.
exs: My client left a really generous tip.
The restaurant gives generous portions.

items.ex: Ask someone out means to invite someone on a date. People say he asked me out. Take someone out is the actual going out.
exs: My coworker finally asked her crush out.
He was too shy to ask her out.

items.ex: Turn down means to say no to an offer or invitation. People say turn down a job, or turn someone down. It's more casual than decline.
exs: I had to turn down a bridal party booking because I was too busy.
She turned down the job offer because the pay was too low.

items.ex: Look forward to means you feel excited about something coming. After it, use a noun or an -ing verb: I'm looking forward to seeing you.
exs: I'm looking forward to seeing you at your next fill.
I'm really looking forward to the weekend.

items.ex: See someone can mean you're dating them. People ask, are you seeing anyone? It's softer than being in a relationship. Careful: see a doctor just means visit a doctor.
exs: My client is seeing someone new, so she's booking more appointments.
Are you seeing anyone right now?

items.ex: Afford means you have enough money to pay for something. People usually say can afford or can't afford: I can't afford a new car.
exs: Some clients can't afford a full set every two weeks, so I offer smaller fills.
We can't afford a bigger apartment right now.
